l: Paris, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_a beardless youth [in the painting] Paris is depicted above Sarpedon and Memnon as a beardless youth. He claps his hands like a rustic, apparently trying to attract Penthesilea’s attention.

l: Penthesilea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Penthesilea is a maiden shown with a Scythian bow and leopard skin, looking at Paris while despising and jeering at him as a boy.

l: shrine of Isis near Tithorea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: A shrine of Isis about 40 stades from the temple of Æsculapius, described as the holiest Greek shrine to the Egyptian goddess; Tithorea’s people live away from it, and only dream-invited people may approach.

l: Festival of Isis at Tithorea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Festival of Isis is held twice yearly, in Spring and Autumn. Before it, the shrine is secretly purified and old remains buried. Traders sell slaves and goods; at noon worshippers sacrifice oxen and deer, but not swine, sheep, or goats. Wrapped victims are processed and burned, tents burn, and participants depart.

l: blockade of Elatea by the Romans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The blockade of Elatea by the Romans reduced the town after it remained faithful to Philip, the son of Demetrius, rather than revolting from the Macedonians.

l: barbarians from Pontus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The barbarians from Pontus joined Taxilus in attacking Elatea. The Elateans held out against them, and their resistance helped earn the town freedom and immunity from taxation from the Romans.

l: Costoboci, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Costoboci, a piratical tribe, overran Greece and reached Elatea, where Mnesibulus led resistance, slew many, and died in battle.

l: Mnesibulus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Mnesibulus was a victorious defender and runner: after winning several contests, including the stadium and double course carrying his shield, he led picked men against the Costoboci at Elatea, killed many, and died in battle; a brazen statue commemorated him.

l: Athene Cranæa, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: has_temple temple of Athene Cranæa Athene Cranæa has a temple about 20 stades from Elatea. Her statue was armed for battle and imitated the shield of Athene in the Parthenon at Athens.

l: temple of Athene Cranæa, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The temple of Athene Cranæa stands on a mostly precipitous hill crest reached by an easy uphill road from Elatea, with porticoes and chambers for ministers; its priest, chosen from youths, serves five years, resides there, and bathes traditionally.

l: statue of Athene Cranæa, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Statue of Athene Cranæa, made by the sons of Polycles, is armed for battle and bears a shield imitating Athene’s Parthenon shield.

l: Temple of Apollo at Abæ, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The ancient temple of Apollo at Abæ was burnt by Xerxes’ army and later by the Thebans during the Phocian War, when Phocian fugitives sheltered there. Most ruinous among fire-damaged buildings, it stood near Adrian’s smaller temple with bronze statues.

l: Temple of Demeter Stiritis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: A temple at Stiris, built of unbaked brick, was dedicated to Demeter Stiritis and housed her Pentelican marble, torch-bearing statue.

l: Persian destruction of Abæ, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_a destruction [by fire] The Persian destruction of Abæ included the burning of its Temple of Apollo by Xerxes’ army. The temple was later consumed altogether by a Theban fire during the Phocian War.

l: coccus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Coccus, about the size of the white thorn, with darker, softer leaves than the mastich-tree, grows between Stiris and Ambrosus; its grub-filled berry is gathered for blood used in dyeing wool.

l: double walls of Ambrosus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The double walls of Ambrosus are a fortification surrounding Ambrosus, built by the Thebans during the war against Philip and the Macedonians. Made of the district’s black, very strong stone for immediate defence, they consist of two plain walls a fathom apart, without towers, battlements, or embellishment; where intact, each is 2½ fathoms high.

l: temple of Dictynnæan Artemis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_located_near Ambrosus [on the right after the road from Ambrosus to Anticyra becomes level] A temple of Dictynnæan Artemis stands about two stades from Ambrosus on the road to Anticyra. Its statue of the goddess is made in the Aeginetan style from black stone.

l: Dictynnæan Artemis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_held_in_highest_honour_by Ambrosus [among the people] Dictynnæan Artemis is held in the highest honour by the people of Ambrosus. Her statue in the temple near Ambrosus is of black stone and Aeginetan workmanship.

l: Bulis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Bulis is a town bordering Phocis, founded by Bulon and colonized from ancient Doris. On high ground, it lay 80 stades from Thisbe and about seven by land from its port. Its people were linked to Philomelus and the Phocians’ impiety; many caught shellfish for purple dye. It had temples, a god, and Saunion well.

l: war against Cirrha, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: has_leader Clisthenes [king of Sicyon] The Amphictyones waged war against Cirrha after its people committed impious acts against Apollo and ravaged his sacred territory. Clisthenes led the war, while Solon assisted with his counsel.

l: siege of Cirrha, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The siege of Cirrha ends when Solon’s river Plistus stratagem with hellebore causes incessant diarrhoea; unable to man the walls, Cirrha is captured by the Amphictyones.

l: Myonia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Myonia is a town above Amphissa, about 30 stades away and facing the mainland. It honors Zeus with a shield at Olympia and has high-ground sanctuaries: a grove and altar of the Mild Deities for nightly sacrifices, and Poseidonium.

l: Œanthea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Œanthea is a town near the sea, placed under the Achæans of Patræ by Augustus. It has a temple of Aphrodite and, above it, a cypress-and-pine grove with a temple and statue of Artemis and time-obscured paintings; its name may derive from a woman or Nymph.

l: origin of the name Ozolian, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Ozolian is a name whose origin is explained by competing traditions. One tells of Orestheus burying a piece of wood born from a bitch, from which a vine grew and gave the Locrians their name; others invoke Nessus, river smell, asphodel, Aborigines, or untanned hides.

This document is a mythological genealogy and narrative history, organized chiefly through divine and heroic families. It begins with Sky and Earth: Sky fathers the Hundred-handed, Cyclopes, and Titans, is overthrown by Cronus, and Cronus in turn is defeated by Zeus after Zeus frees the prisoners of Tartarus. Zeus, Poseidon, and Pluto divide rule over sky, sea, and Hades. The account then surveys Zeus’s unions and children, the births and deeds of Apollo, Artemis, Athena, Persephone’s division of the year between Pluto and the gods, the Giants and Typhon, and Prometheus, Deucalion, and the restoration of humankind after the flood. It next develops Greek genealogies through Hellen and his descendants, including Calydon, Athamas, Tyro, Pelias, Admetus, and Jason. Jason’s expedition for the Golden Fleece occupies a major sequence: he gathers the Argonauts, reaches Colchis, wins Medea’s help, obtains the fleece, and returns to Iolcus. Medea later causes Pelias’s death, is abandoned by Jason for Glauce, kills Glauce and her own children, flees to Athens, and eventually restores Aeetes in Colchis. The narrative then follows the Inachean line through Io, Danaus, Acrisius, Perseus, and Amphitryon to Hercules. Hercules’ madness, service to Eurystheus, and labours form the largest heroic section, from the Nemean lion and Lernaean hydra to the apples of the Hesperides and Cerberus. Afterward he conquers Troy and other cities, marries Deianira, and dies through the poisoned tunic made from Nessus’s blood; he is taken to heaven, becomes immortal, and marries Hebe. His descendants, the Heraclids, eventually return to and divide the Peloponnese. Finally, the account turns to Agenor’s house: Europa, Minos and the Minotaur, Cadmus and Thebes, Dionysus, and the Theban disasters of Oedipus, Eteocles, Polynices, the Seven, and the Epigoni. It closes with Pelasgian and Arcadian lines, including Lycaon’s impiety, Callisto, Auge, Telephus, and Atalanta.

Apollodorus is identified with The Library in the heading of the unit. Apollodorus records that Eurystheus assigned Hercules the eleventh labour of fetching the golden apples and describes their location and guardians.
is_a work The Library presents Uranus as the first ruler of the entire universe and recounts his marriage to Earth and the birth of the Hecatoncheires.

Sky, also called Uranus, was the first ruler of the whole world and entire universe. He married Earth and, with her, fathered the Hundred-handed, Cyclopes, Titans, Titanides, and others including Cronus and the giants. He bound the Cyclopes in Tartarus. Later the Titans attacked him, and Cronus cut off his genitals and overthrew him.

Earth is a goddess and prophetic deity, married to and consort of Sky. With Sky she bears the Hecatoncheires, Hundred-handed, Cyclopes, Titans, Titanides, and, when vexed by the Titans, the Giants. Grieved that Sky cast children into Tartarus, she persuades the Titans to attack Sky and gives Cronus an adamantine sickle. She prophesies Zeus’s victory if he obtains allies from Tartarus. Seeking a potion or herb to save the Giants from a mortal, she is thwarted by Zeus. After their defeat, she joins Tartarus, bears Typhon in Cilicia, and is cleft by Zeus’s thunderbolt.
The Hecatoncheires are Briareus, Gyges, and Cottus, among the first children of Uranus and Earth; each is a being of unsurpassable size and power with one hundred hands and fifty heads.
is_a Hundred-handed Briareus was one of the Hecatoncheires born to Uranus and Earth. He was extraordinarily large and powerful and had one hundred hands and fifty heads.
Gyges was one of the Hecatoncheires born to Uranus and Earth. He was extraordinarily large and powerful and had one hundred hands and fifty heads.
is_a Hundred-handed Cottus was one of the Hecatoncheires born to Uranus and Earth. He was extraordinarily large and powerful and had one hundred hands and fifty heads.

Cronus, youngest of the Titans, overthrows Sky with an adamantine sickle and becomes ruler. Married to Rhea, he fathers Demeter, Hera, Pluto, Poseidon, and Zeus. Fearing a prophecy that a son will dethrone him, he imprisons the Cyclopes and swallows his children, but mistakes a wrapped stone for Zeus. Forced by Metis’s drug to disgorge the stone and children, he faces war from Zeus and them.

Giants are children of Earth and Sky, born in Phlegra or Pallene. They have matchless bulk, invincible might, terrible forms, long locks, and dragon-scaled feet; they hurl rocks and burning oaks at the sky. Porphyrion and Alcyoneus excel among them, with Alcyoneus immortal in his native land. In war with the gods, Zeus strikes many with thunderbolts and Heracles shoots the dying Giants.

Cyclopes are a group whose members have one forehead eye; after Zeus frees them from bonds by killing Campe, they give Zeus thunder, lightning, and a thunderbolt, arm Pluto and Poseidon, and fortify Tiryns for Proetus.

l: the marriage of Sky and Earth, The Library
s: is_a marriage The marriage of Sky and Earth is presented as a myth in which Sky and Earth are joined. The text notes that this myth is widespread among lower races.
Human beings are made from water and earth; a flood nearly destroys them, then stones become men and women.

Tartarus is a gloomy place in Hades, as far from Earth as Earth is from Sky. Sky and Cronus shut the Cyclopes there; Zeus releases certain allies from it, while defeated Titans are imprisoned under the Hundred-handers’ guard.

Hades was the place from which Hercules was ordered to bring Cerberus. Hercules descends into Hades through the entrance at Taenarum. The souls flee from him except Meleager and Medusa, and near the gates he finds Theseus and Pirithous bound. Hercules later returns Cerberus to Hades after displaying him to Eurystheus.

The Titans, children of Sky and Earth, include Ocean, Coeus, Hyperion, Crius, Iapetus, and youngest Cronus. Urged by Earth, all but Ocean attack Sky, free brothers from Tartarus, and give Cronus rule. They later fight Zeus for ten years, lose, and are imprisoned in Tartarus.
Rhea, a Titanide and Cronus’s sister-wife, bore their children. After Cronus swallowed them, she fled pregnant to Crete, gave birth to Zeus in Dicte’s cave, and deceived Cronus with a wrapped stone.

A goddess searches for Persephone with torches; after learning Pluto abducted her, she leaves heaven in anger, comes to Eleusis disguised as a woman, and sits on Laughless Rock beside the Well of the Fair Dances.

Hera is married to Zeus and is parent of Hebe, Ilithyia, Ares, and, without intercourse in this account, Hephaestus. Her marriage is marked by Earth’s gift of golden apples; she has a wooden image and a precinct where Sidero took refuge. Much of her story concerns forceful, often jealous action: she hunts Leto across the earth, casts Side into Hades for rival beauty, pursues Io after detecting Zeus’s seduction, sets Argus the All-seeing over the cow, sends a gadfly, and has the Curetes remove Epaphus. She delays Heracles’ birth, drives Hercules mad, sends storms against him, and is punished by Zeus, who hangs her from Olympus; later she is reconciled with Hercules. She sends the Sphinx against Thebes, causes Callisto’s death through Artemis, blinds Tiresias after his answer to her and Zeus, and disperses cattle with a gadfly. She also assists the Argonauts, joins a conspiracy against Zeus, faces Porphyrion’s attack and Ephialtes’ courtship, and is opposed to Epaphus.

Pluto receives a helmet from the Cyclopes and gains dominion over Hades when sovereignty is divided. He falls in love with Persephone, secretly carries her off with Zeus’s help, binds her through a pomegranate seed, marries her, and permits Hercules to take Cerberus without weapons.

Poseidon is a deity whose defining domain is the sea, allotted to him when sovereignty was divided by lot; the Cyclopes gave him a trident. He acts through sea power, springs, floods, monsters, and bulls, while also taking forms and fathering many children. He gave Orion power to stride across the sea and, according to Pherecydes, was Orion’s father; he also had an underground house made by Hephaestus for Oenopion. Married to Amphitrite and parent of Triton and Rhode, he fathered Hopleus, Nireus, Epopeus, Aloeus, and Triops by Canace; Otus and Ephialtes by Iphimedia; Pelias and Neleus through Tyro after resembling Enipeus; Belus and Agenor with Libya; Pegasus with Medusa; Eurypylus by Astypalaea; and Arion on Demeter. He granted Periclymenus shape-changing power. He created Nisyrus from Cos, dried springs in anger at Inachus, then revealed Lerna’s springs to Amymone. With Apollo he fortified Pergamum for Laomedon, but after withheld wages he sent a sea monster; another account says he served Laomedon as Zeus’s punishment. He joined Hera and Athena in a conspiracy against Zeus. His anger also brought a flood and monster after Cassiopeia, and punished Minos by making a bull savage and causing Pasiphae to desire it.

l: prophecy of Cronus's dethronement, The Library
s: The prophecy stated that Cronus would be deprived of his rule by his own child. Earth and Sky foretold it, causing Cronus to swallow each child born to him until Rhea concealed Zeus.

Crete was the place to which Zeus, in the form of a tame bull, carried Europa. Zeus fathered Minos, Sarpedon, and Rhadamanthys with her there. Crete was ruled by Minos, who passed laws there and extended his dominion over almost all the islands. It was also the destination of Europa and the place where Asterius raised her children.
Dicte was the place in Crete where Rhea gave birth to Zeus in a cave. She entrusted Zeus to the Curetes and the nymphs Adrastia and Ida to be raised there.

Zeus is a god, son of Cronus and Rhea, secretly born in the cave of Dicte and nursed and guarded by nymphs, Curetes, and Amalthea while Cronus is deceived with a stone. Once grown, Zeus allies with Metis, frees the Cyclopes, receives thunder, lightning, and the thunderbolt, defeats Cronus and the Titans with Cronus’s disgorged children, and gains sovereignty over the sky. He becomes a powerful ruler and punisher: he fights Giants and Typhon, uses thunderbolts against enemies and offenders, punishes Prometheus, Salmoneus, Lycaon and his sons, Capaneus, and Hera, and acts against the Curetes after Epaphus disappears. He also directs or intervenes in events involving Persephone, the Argonauts, Heracles, Tiresias, Cadmus and Harmonia, and others. His family and sexual unions are central. Zeus marries Hera and fathers Hebe, Ilithyia, and Ares; he fathers many further children by goddesses and mortal women, including the Seasons, Fates, Graces, Persephone, the Muses, Athena, Apollo, Artemis, Tityus, Hellen, Aethlius, Argos, Epaphus, Perseus, Hercules, Minos, Sarpedon, Rhadamanthys, and others attributed to him in particular accounts. He repeatedly changes form or appearance in these affairs: into gold for Danae, Amphitryon’s likeness for Alcmena, a tame bull for Europa, and disguises associated with Artemis or Apollo for Callisto. He transforms or causes transformations, including Io into a white cow, Callisto into a bear, Ceyx and Alcyone into birds, Dionysus into a kid, and Laelaps and the vixen into stone. The record closes with Zeus testing Lycaon’s family in a day-labourer’s form, punishing their impiety, and concealing Callisto from Hera.

Metis, Ocean’s daughter and Zeus’s consort, helps Zeus defeat Cronus by administering a drug that makes him disgorge the stone and swallowed children. She changes shape to avoid Zeus, becomes pregnant by him, and is swallowed by Zeus because he fears her child’s future rule.

l: children swallowed by Cronus, The Library
s: The children swallowed by Cronus are disgorged after he takes the drug given by Metis. They assist Zeus in his war against Cronus and the Titans.

l: war against Cronus and the Titans, The Library
s: The war lasts ten years. Earth prophesies victory to Zeus if he has as allies those who were hurled down to Tartarus, and Zeus and his allies ultimately defeat the Titans.

is_divided_among Zeus [by lot; dominion of the sky] The gods cast lots for sovereignty after defeating the Titans. Zeus receives dominion over the sky, Poseidon dominion over the sea, and Pluto dominion in Hades.
Asteria, daughter of Coeus, escapes Zeus’s amorous advances as a quail by throwing herself into the sea; the island once called Asteria is later called Delos.
Leto, daughter of Coeus, is pursued by Hera after her union with Zeus, reaches Delos, gives birth to Artemis and Apollo, and incites them against Niobe’s children.
Perses, Hecate's parent with Asteria, deposed Aeetes and took his kingdom before Medea killed him and restored it.
Atlas, among the Hyperboreans, bears the sky as a burden. Relieved by Hercules while obtaining three golden apples from the Hesperides, he is tricked into taking the sphere back.

Prometheus, creator of human beings and father of Deucalion, moulds people from water and earth and secretly gives them fire. Punished by Zeus, he is nailed or chained to the Caucasus, where an eagle daily devours his regrowing liver. Hercules shoots the eagle and releases him, with Chiron dying as a substitute.
The Phorcides, Enyo, Pephredo, and Dino, are daughters of Phorcus and Ceto and sisters of the Gorgons; sharing one eye and tooth, they guide Perseus to the nymphs after he takes them.
The Gorgons are Stheno, Euryale, and Medusa, winged beings with scaled heads, tusks, and brazen hands who turn beholders to stone; Medusa alone is mortal.
The Nereids became angry with Cassiopeia after she claimed superiority in beauty. Poseidon shared their anger and sent a flood and a sea monster against the land.

has_son Parthenopaeus [according to an alternative genealogy with Atalanta] Ares was said to be the father of the dragon that guarded the spring near Thebes. Cadmus served Ares for an eternal year as atonement for killing the dragon.
Born to Zeus and Dione, Aphrodite becomes wrathful toward Clio, makes Dawn perpetually love, and gives Melanion golden apples used against Atalanta.
Persephone, Demeter’s daughter and Pluto’s wife, is secretly taken to the underworld, eats a pomegranate seed, and thereafter divides each year between Pluto and the gods.
Muses, daughters of Zeus and Mnemosyne, include Calliope through Polymnia; they teach the Sphinx’s riddle and defeat Thamyris in music, taking his eyes and minstrelsy.
Calliope, first listed among the Muses, bore Linus and Orpheus to Oeagrus or nominally Apollo; some also said Rhesus was her son.

Apollo, born on Delos after Artemis, is named nominal father of Linus and Orpheus with Calliope, and loved Hyacinth, whom he accidentally killed with a discus. He learned prophecy from Pan, came to Delphi, killed Python, and took over its oracle. He killed Tityus with Artemis’s aid, defeated Marsyas by turning his lyre upside down, then hanged and flayed him. He met Melampus at the Alpheus, aided Admetus by yoking a lion and boar and obtaining death-substitution from the Fates, and received Manto at Delphi. With Poseidon, he served Laomedon and fortified Pergamum for wages; when unpaid, he sent pestilence. With Artemis he killed Niobe’s male children. His oracle predicted victory for the Epigoni under Alcmaeon and instructed Alcmaeon to kill Eriphyle.

Hercules is a mortal hero, son of Zeus and descendant of Perseus, whose divine parentage is visibly apparent. He is brother to Iphicles, trained in chariot-driving, wrestling, archery, and fencing, armed with divine gifts, a self-cut club, and arrows dipped in hydra gall. He marries Megara and has children by her, but after killing his children in madness he is purified and compelled to serve Eurystheus at Tiryns for twelve years. There he performs the labours: killing the Nemean lion and hydra, capturing beasts, cleansing Augeas’s yard, defeating enemies including Hippolyte and Geryon, obtaining the golden apples, and bringing Cerberus from Hades without weapons. He is purified and initiated at Eleusis before this descent, then returns Cerberus and gives Megara to Iolaus. His career also includes aiding Zeus against Giants and Typhon, releasing Prometheus, ravaging Pylus, restoring Alcestis according to one account, and being left in Mysia while seeking Hylas. After killing Iphitus in madness, he is purified and sold to Omphale for three years, during which he kills Syleus, buries Icarus, and is said to join the voyage to Colchis and the Calydonian hunt. He later leads an army against Troy, captures it, kills Laomedon and his sons except Podarces, and gives Hesione to Telamon. He marries Deianira after defeating Achelous, campaigns and captures cities, then accepts exile after accidentally killing Eunomus. At Trachis he defeats enemies and captures Oechalia, but Deianira’s treatment of his tunic with Nessus’s blood and the hydra’s poison destroys his body. He builds a pyre on Oeta, gives his bow to Poeas, and is carried in a cloud with thunder to heaven, where he becomes immortal and marries Hebe.

Orpheus, son of Calliope and Oeagrus or nominally Apollo, was a musician whose song moved stones and trees. Married to Eurydice, he sought her in Hades but lost her again by looking back. He instituted Dionysian mysteries, was torn apart by Maenads, and buried in Pieria.
Eurydice, Lacedaemon’s daughter and Orpheus’s wife, dies from a snake bite and returns to Hades when Orpheus looks back.

Dionysus is a god, protected by Zeus and conveyed by Hermes to Nysa. He discovers the vine and has rites, but Hera drives him into madness. He wanders through Egypt and Syria, is received by Proteus, then reaches Cybela, where Rhea purifies him, teaches him initiation rites, and gives him a costume. He travels through Thrace, India, Thebes, and Argos, driving Lycurgus and women mad and forcing women on Cithaeron into bacchic frenzy. He defeats pirates by transforming their ship and them, brings Semele from Hades, and ascends to heaven with Thyone.
is_loved_by Apollo [as a beloved male] Hyacinth was the son of Clio and Pierus. Apollo loved him and accidentally killed him by throwing a discus.
Thamyris, a beautiful minstrel and son of Philammon and Argiope, loved Hyacinth, fathered Rhesus, challenged the Muses in music, and, defeated, lost his eyes and minstrelsy.

l: musical contest between Apollo and Marsyas, The Library
s: is_a contest [over music] Apollo and Marsyas agreed that the victor could do whatever he wished to the defeated contestant. Apollo turned his lyre upside down and ordered Marsyas to do the same with his pipes; when Marsyas could not, Apollo was judged the victor and killed him.

Hephaestus was born to Hera without intercourse, though Homer says that Zeus was also his father. Zeus cast him from heaven when he came to Hera’s aid, and he fell on Lemnos and was lamed in his legs before Thetis saved him.

Troy is a city suffering from the anger of Apollo and Poseidon when Hercules touches there after fighting the Amazons. After Laomedon refuses promised payment, Hercules threatens war, sails to Ilium with an army, and captures the besieged city after Telamon breaches its wall; Laomedon and his sons except Podarces are killed.
Lemnos, a place, is temporarily without men after their massacre, ruled by Hypsipyle, visited by the Argonauts, who sleep with its women and sail onward.

Athena emerges fully armed from the top of Zeus’s head after it is struck with an axe. She throws away pipes because they disfigure her face; Marsyas later finds and uses them against Apollo. In the war against the Giants, she summons Heracles, advises him about Alcyoneus, throws Sicily on Enceladus, and flays Pallas to make protective covering. She guides Perseus to the Phorcides and directs his hand as he beheads Medusa using a brazen shield; she later receives the Gorgon’s head and places it in her shield. According to Homer, she joins Poseidon and Hera in a conspiracy against Zeus. According to Pherecydes, she blinds Tiresias after he sees her naked, then cleanses his ears and gives him a cornel-wood staff when she cannot restore his sight. She gives brazen castanets to Hercules, returns the apples of the Hesperides, and withholds immortality medicine from Tydeus after his act disgusts her. Her precinct, where Auge is priestess, becomes tied to an impiety and barren land.

Diomedes is described as both the son of Tydeus and Deipyle and a Thracian king, son of Ares and Cyrene, who rules the war-like Bistones and owns man-eating mares. He secretly comes from Argos, kills nearly all Agrius’s sons, gives Oeneus’s kingdom to Andraemon, and buries Oeneus at Oenoe. After the mares’ capture, Hercules kills him.

Achelous is a figure who takes the form of a bull while contending with Hercules for Deianira, loses a horn, and exchanges Amalthea’s horn to recover it. Later, at his springs, he purifies Alcmaeon, gives him Callirrhoe as wife, and directs Alcmaeon’s sons to dedicate a necklace and robe at Delphi.

was_formerly_called Asteria Delos was formerly called Asteria. Leto reached Delos while fleeing Hera and gave birth there first to Artemis and later to Apollo; Artemis also killed Orion there, and Dawn brought Orion there.

Artemis is a maiden devoted to the chase who remains a virgin and has the Cerynitian hind as a sacred animal. Born on Delos before Apollo, she helps Leto give birth to him. She kills Gration, Tityus, Orion, and Niobe’s female children, the latter after Niobe boasts of her children. When Actaeon sees her bathing, she turns him into a deer and causes his dogs to devour him. Callisto is her hunting companion, but Artemis shoots her as a wild animal through Hera’s persuasion or because Callisto breaks her vow. Artemis is wooed by Otus and is omitted from the sacrifice at Admetus and Alcestis’s marriage.
Delphi is the place of an oracle: Themis delivers oracles there until Apollo arrives, kills Python guarding the chasm, and later Oedipus and Hercules consult it, with Hercules asking where to dwell.
guards oracle of Delphi Python was a snake guarding the oracle at Delphi. It prevented Apollo from approaching the chasm, but Apollo killed it and took over the oracle.
The oracle of Delphi was being delivered by Themis when Apollo arrived. After killing Python, Apollo took over the oracle.
Tityus, gigantic son of Zeus and Elare, rose from beneath the earth, attacked Leto from lust, was shot by her children, and in Hades vultures ate his heart.

is_a son of Olympus Marsyas was the son of Olympus and found the pipes that Athena had thrown away. He competed musically with Apollo, lost because he could not turn his pipes upside down, and was hanged from a pine and flayed by Apollo.

Orion is a gigantic, earth-born figure, though Pherecydes calls him son of Poseidon and Euryale. He marries Side, crosses the sea by Poseidon's gift, is blinded by Oenopion, regains sight through the sun, is carried to Delos by Dawn, and is killed by Artemis.

blinds Orion [while Orion was drunk and asleep] Oenopion's daughter Merope was wooed by Orion. Oenopion made Orion drunk, blinded him while he slept, and threw him onto the beach; Poseidon later prepared an underground house for Oenopion.
Demeter searches all over the earth for Persephone.

Demeter comes to Eleusis in the likeness of a woman. She first sits on the Laughless Rock beside the Well of the Fair Dances and then goes to the house of Celeus. Eleusis was where Hercules went to Eumolpus because he wished to be initiated.
Fire, hidden in a fennel stalk and stolen by Prometheus, is given to human beings; Zeus punishes Prometheus.
Pluto gives Persephone a pomegranate seed to eat. Persephone eats it without foreseeing the consequence.

l: the underworld division of Persephone’s time, The Library
s: Persephone is compelled to remain one-third of every year with Pluto, spending the rest with the gods.

l: the abduction of Persephone, The Library
s: is_performed_by Pluto [with the help of Zeus and secretly] Pluto secretly abducts Persephone with the help of Zeus. Demeter learns from the people of Hermion that Pluto carried her off.

l: Demeter’s search for Persephone, The Library
s: takes_place_on earth [all over the earth, by night and day] Demeter searches for Persephone throughout the earth with torches by night and day. Her search leads her to Hermion and then to Eleusis.
Erythia, an island near the ocean now called Gadira, is inhabited by Geryon and holds Geryon’s red kine.

Ephialtes, fathered by Poseidon and Iphimedia and one of the Aloads, wooed Hera and helped threaten the gods. In Naxos, Artemis disguised as a deer caused him and Otus to spear each other, killing him.

Eurytus, prince and king of Oechalia and a general of Elis with Cteatus, offers Iole to an archery victor but refuses her to Hercules, fearing for his children. He suspects Hercules of cattle theft and rejects compensation for Iphitus’s murder. Hercules later attacks, kills Eurytus and his sons, and takes Oechalia.

l: the cap of Hades, The Library
s: makes_invisible Perseus [to others while worn by him] The cap of Hades belonged to the nymphs. When Perseus wore it, he could see whom he wished while remaining unseen by others.

Hermes, also called Argiphontes after killing Argus the All-seeing on Zeus’s order, wears Hades’ helmet and kills Hippolytus in battle. He gives Perseus an adamantine sickle and Amphion a lyre, identifies Medusa as an empty phantom, purifies Danaus’s daughters with Athena, and guides Perseus to the Phorcides.

Typhon is a vast hybrid of man and beast, born in Cilicia from Earth and Tartarus after the Giants’ defeat. Larger and stronger than the Giants, he has a human shape to the thighs, wings, dragon heads, serpent coils, and fire-flashing eyes. Zeus wounds and pursues him, but Typhon overpowers Zeus and hides his severed hand and foot sinews in the Corycian cave. After Hermes and Aegipan restore Zeus, Zeus pursues Typhon until defeating and burying him under Mount Etna.

Egypt is a country named after Egyptus, who subjugated the Melampods. Dionysus wandered through it and was received by its king Proteus; afterward, Hercules traversed Egypt after Libya, when Busiris ruled.
Thrace contains Salmydessus and is traversed by Dionysus as he hastens against the Indians, later reaching Thebes.

l: war of the gods and Giants, The Library
s: is_fought_by Hercules [alongside the gods] The war begins when the Giants attack the sky by hurling rocks and burning oaks. The gods receive an oracle that the Giants can be destroyed only with the aid of a mortal, so Zeus summons Heracles through Athena. The gods and Heracles defeat the Giants, with each combatant being killed or overcome by various gods, Heracles, or Zeus.
Deucalion, son of Prometheus, rules near Phthia and marries Pyrrha; advised by Prometheus, they survive the Flood in a chest, land on Parnassus, and create men from stones.
Pyrrha, daughter of Epimetheus and Pandora, marries Deucalion, survives the Flood with him, and creates women from thrown stones.
Deucalion constructs it on Prometheus's advice, provisions it, and enters with Pyrrha; it floats over the sea for nine days and nights during the Flood.
is_flooded_by the Flood [the greater part] Zeus floods most of Greece with heavy rain, destroying its inhabitants except for those who escape to nearby high mountains.

Peloponnese, a land also called Apia and Argos, received Xuthus, where he fathered Achaeus and Ion; it was ruled by Phoroneus, struck by plague after the Heraclids' return, then conquered and divided by them.
receives Deucalion [after the Flood] Deucalion and Pyrrha drift to Mount Parnassus in the chest. They land there after the rains stop.
Stones thrown by Deucalion and Pyrrha over their heads at Zeus's bidding become men from Deucalion's and women from Pyrrha's.

Deucalion’s flood occurs after Nyctimus takes the kingdom, when Zeus pours heavy rain from heaven, possibly because of Lycaon’s sons’ impiety. It destroys most of Greece and its people, but Deucalion and Pyrrha survive in their chest.

l: the theft of fire, The Library
s: The theft of fire is committed by Prometheus when he secretly takes fire and gives it to human beings. Zeus punishes him for the theft by having him bound on Mount Caucasus.
Hellen, a mythical ancestor possibly born from Zeus, fathered Dorus, Xuthus, and Aeolus with Orseis, named the Greeks Hellenes, and divided the country among his sons.
Dorus, son of Hellen and Orseis, receives the country beyond Peloponnese and names its inhabitants Dorians after himself.
Xuthus, son of Hellen and Orseis, received Peloponnese and fathered Achaeus and Ion by Creusa.

Aeolus, son of Hellen and Orseis, ruled the regions around Thessaly and named their inhabitants Aeolians. With his wife Enarete, he had seven sons, Cretheus, Sisyphus, Athamas, Salmoneus, Deion, Magnes, and Perieres, and five daughters: Canace, Alcyone, Pisidice, Calyce, and Perimede.
are_called Hellenes [after Hellen] The people called Greeks were renamed Hellenes by Hellen.
The Hellenes were the people whom Hellen named after himself from among those previously called Greeks.
Brother of Salmoneus, Cretheus raised and married Tyro, founded Pherae and Iolcus, and fathered Aeson, Amythaon, and Pheres.

Sisyphus, son of Aeolus, founds Ephyra, later called Corinth, marries Merope, and has Glaucus. After revealing Zeus's secret abduction of Aegina to Asopus, he is punished in Hades by repeatedly rolling a stone upward only for it to rebound.

Athamas, son of Aeolus and ruler of Boeotia, fathers Phrixus and Helle by Nephele, then Learchus and Melicertes by his second wife Ino. Amid dearth he consults Delphi and is forced to offer Phrixus for sacrifice, but Nephele rescues him. After madness and Hera’s wrath cost him Learchus and Melicertes, he is banished and settles Athamantia.

Salmoneus first dwells in Thessaly, then founds a city in Elis. Impiously claiming to be Zeus, he redirects sacrifices and imitates thunder and lightning with hides, kettles, and torches. Zeus destroys him by thunderbolt, along with his city and all its inhabitants.
Otus, one of the Aloads, wooed Artemis, helped threaten the gods, and died in Naxos when Artemis as a deer made him and Ephialtes spear each other.

Aloads were Otus and Ephialtes, sons of Poseidon and Iphimedia. Growing extraordinarily fast, they became enormous, opposed the gods, and piled Pelion on Ossa toward Olympus to reach heaven. They threatened sea and land, imprisoned Ares, and Artemis killed them by deception.
Dionysus wished to be transported from Icaria to Naxos. The Tyrrhenian pirates carried him past Naxos while attempting to take him to Asia to sell him.

Endymion was the son of Calyce and Aethlius, though some said he was born from Zeus. He led Aeolians from Thessaly, settled Elis, and was loved by Selene; Zeus granted him the choice of what he wished, and he chose eternal sleep while remaining immortal and ageless.

is_a city [taken by Hercules] Elis sends the Molionides to participate in the sacrifices at the third Isthmian festival. Hercules ambushes and kills them at Cleonae, then marches against Elis and captures the city.

Aetolus was the son of Endymion and either a Naiad nymph or Iphianassa. After killing Apis, son of Phoroneus, he fled to the land of the Curetes, killed Phthias and Apollo's sons Dorus, Laodocus, and Polypoetes, and named the country Aetolia after himself.
Phoroneus, son of Inachus and Melia, ruled the land later called the Peloponnese and fathered Apis and Niobe by Teledice.
Aetolia was named after Aetolus, who had fled there and killed those who received him, including Phthias and Apollo's sons Dorus, Laodocus, and Polypoetes.
Oxylus, son of Andraemon from Aetolia, returns from exile on a one-eyed horse, is chosen by oracle as guide of the Heraclids, and leads them to defeat the enemy.
Agenor goes to Phoenicia, marries Telephassa, and fathers four children; after Europa disappears, he orders his sons to search without returning until they find her.

Apis, son of Phoroneus and fellow child with Niobe of Teledice, became a stern tyrant, naming the Peloponnese Apia. Childless, he was killed in a conspiracy by Thelxion and Telchis; after death he was deemed a god and called Sarapis.
Amythaon, son of Cretheus and Tyro, dwelt in Pylus, married Idomene, and fathered Bias and Melampus.

is_a son of Agenor Porthaon and Euryte had sons named Oeneus, Agrius, Alcathous, Melas, and Leucopaeus, and a daughter named Sterope. Sterope was said to have become the mother of the Sirens by Achelous.
Evenus was the river Hercules and Deianeira reached while traveling toward Trachis. Hercules crossed it himself, while Nessus ferried Deianeira.

Thestius, son of Demonice and Ares, fathered daughters Althaea, Leda, and Hypermnestra and sons Iphiclus, Evippus, Plexippus, and Eurypylus by Eurythemis; after his sons claimed a boar skin, Meleager killed them.
Messene is the third territory assigned. Cresphontes obtains it through his stratagem in the drawing of lots, and its sign is a fox, interpreted as indicating wily rulers.

Althaea, daughter of Thestius and wife of Oeneus, is mother of Meleager and Deianira. She hides the brand on which Meleager’s life depends, then, grieving her brothers’ deaths, burns it and causes his death; afterward Oeneus marries Periboea.
Hypermnestra, Danaus's eldest daughter, was allotted and later united to Lynceus; she spared him because he respected her virginity, was imprisoned by Danaus, and became mother of Abas.

Oeneus ruled Calydon, first received a vine-plant from Dionysus, and was married to Althaea and later Periboea, by whom or Gorge he had Tydeus. After failing to sacrifice to Artemis, he organized the Calydonian boar hunt. He was imprisoned and tormented by Agrius’s sons, restored by Diomedes, then killed by surviving sons of Agrius; Diomedes buried him at Argos.

Deianira is Oeneus’s daughter and Hercules’s wife. At Calydon, Hercules seeks and wins her in marriage by defeating Achelous. Traveling with Hercules toward Trachis, she is ferried across the Evenus by Nessus, who attempts to assault her and later tells her to make a supposed love charm from material connected with his wound. She keeps it, but fears Hercules will prefer Iole and applies it to his tunic. After seeing what happens to Hercules, she hangs herself.

Meleager, son of Oeneus and Althaea, though possibly Ares’s, became an invulnerable man whose life depended on a burning brand. He led the killing of Artemis’s boar and gave its skin to Atalanta, then killed Thestius’s sons. He died when Althaea burned the brand, or while defending Calydon.
A burning hearth brand determines Meleager’s life: Althaea rescues it from fire and stores it in a chest, then later burns it, causing his immediate death.
A boar sent by Artemis because Oeneus omitted her from a sacrifice, it was extraordinarily large and strong, devastated Calydon, and killed livestock and people until assembled heroes hunted it.

is_a hunt [organized against Artemis’s boar] Oeneus organized the Calydonian boar hunt and promised the boar’s skin to whoever killed it. Atalanta first wounded the boar, Amphiaraus struck its eye, and Meleager killed it with a blow to the flank.
Lynceus, son of Egyptus, survives because Hypermnestra spares him, marries her, becomes king of Argos after Danaus, and fathers Abas.

Theseus, son of Aegeus, was targeted by Medea in Athens, where she was later driven away with her son. After being bound near Hades for joining Pirithous in wooing Persephone, Hercules rescued him. He then led Athens against Thebes, captured the city, and returned the Argive dead for burial.
has_son Medus [with Medea] Aegeus married Medea in Athens, and Medea bore him a son named Medus.

Admetus, son of Pheres, rules Pherae and is served by Apollo. With Apollo’s help he yokes a lion and boar, brings them to Pelias, and obtains Alcestis as his wife. After neglecting Artemis at their marriage, snakes fill his chamber. He is released from death when Alcestis voluntarily dies for him.
is_parent_of Admetus [son] Pheres is one of the children Medea has with Jason. Medea kills him before fleeing Corinth.
has twenty sons Cepheus ruled Ethiopia and was the father of Andromeda and the husband of Cassiopeia. He was forced by the Ethiopians to expose Andromeda to the sea monster.

Lycurgus, son of Dryas, is king and ruler of the Edonians beside the Strymon. He has spouses named Cleophyle, Eurydice, or Eurynome in differing accounts and several children. After insulting and expelling Dionysus, he is driven mad, kills a son, is bound on Mount Pangaeum, and destroyed by horses.

Jason, son of Aeson and Polymede, lives in Iolcus and loses a sandal crossing the Anaurus, fulfilling Pelias’s oracle. Pelias sends him for the Golden Fleece, so Jason has Argus build the Argo and commands the Argonauts. He seeks the fleece from Aeetes, completes Aeetes’s tasks with Medea’s drug, obtains the fleece with her help, and escapes Colchis with Medea and Apsyrtus. After purification by Circe and return to Iolcus, he gives Pelias the fleece and later seeks Medea’s revenge on him. Jason fathers Euneus and Nebrophonus by Hypsipyle, marries Medea, then divorces her and marries Glauce in Corinth.
Aeson is threatened with death by Pelias when Pelias believes the Argonauts will not return. He asks to take his own life and dies while offering a sacrifice and drinking bull’s blood.

Amphitryon, son of Alcaeus in one version, receives a kingdom and Alcmena from Electryon under an oath to preserve her virginity until Electryon returns. While recovering cattle, he accidentally kills Electryon with a rebounding club and is banished by Sthenelus. He goes with Alcmena and Licymnius to Thebes, where Creon purifies him. To marry Alcmena and avenge her brothers, he gathers allies, attempts to rid the Cadmea of the vixen, and conquers the Tafian islands and Teleboans, killing Comaetho and distributing the islands and booty. Husband of Alcmena and father of Iphicles and, in one account, Hercules, he dies bravely fighting the Minyans.
Telamon first breaches Troy’s wall and enters the city during the siege; after its capture, Heracles awards him Hesione.

Atalanta, a daughter of Schoeneus from Arcadia, was exposed because her father wanted male children, suckled by a she-bear, and raised by hunters. A virgin and skilled armed huntress, she killed the centaurs Rhoecus and Hylaeus after they tried to force her, joined the Calydonian boar hunt despite objections, first struck the boar, and received its skin from Meleager after it was taken from her and reclaimed. She also defeated Peleus in wrestling. In her marriage race, she lost to Melanion after stopping for golden apples, married him, and had Parthenopaeus in the main account. She and Melanion became lions after intercourse in Zeus’s precinct. Other accounts name Maenalus as her father and Hippomenes as her spouse.

Amphiaraus, son of Oicles, is a seer who foresees that all expedition participants but Adrastus will die. Opposing the march to Thebes, he is persuaded by Eriphyle to join, hates Tydeus for urging the campaign, and at Nemea interprets Opheltes’s death as an omen while winning leaping and quoit-throwing contests. He orders his sons to kill their mother and march against Thebes, kills Melanippus, then flees until Zeus opens the earth, swallowing him with his chariot and charioteer and making him immortal.

belongs_to Atalanta [according to Meleager's award] The boar skin was promised by Oeneus as the prize for killing the beast. Meleager gave it to Atalanta, but the sons of Thestius seized it, claiming it belonged to them by right of birth; Meleager killed them and restored the skin to Atalanta.

Tydeus is an Aetolian son of Oeneus, born to Periboea according to one account and Gorge according to another. After killing relatives or conspirators against Oeneus, he is banished from and flees Calydon. In Argos he fights Polynices until Adrastus separates them, marries Adrastus’s daughter Deipyle, and fathers Diomedes. He becomes one of the Seven Champions, wins boxing at Nemea, and serves as Adrastus’s envoy to Eteocles; ambushed by fifty men, he kills all but Maeon. In the attack on Thebes, stationed at Crenidian Gate, he is fatally wounded by Melanippus. After consuming Melanippus’s brains, he loses Athena’s intended medicine and dies in Thebes.

Argos is a place of refuge and a kingdom, also the name Argus gave to the Peloponnese and a place linked to Inachus and the river Inachus. It received Tydeus after exile; he married Deipyle there. Diomedes later departed from it with Alcmaeon, attacked the sons of Agrius, and brought Oeneus’s body back for burial at Oenoe. Acrisius ruled Argos in the division with Proetus. Perseus exchanged it for Tiryns with Megapenthes, who ruled the Argives. Lots first assigned it, marked by a toad. Adrastus then sheltered Polynices and assembled champions for war against Thebes.

Adrastus is a son of Talaus and Lysimache, a descendant of Bias and Pero, and king of Argos. With Amphithea he fathers Argia, Deipyle, Aegialia, Aegialeus, and Cyanippus. He stops Polynices and Tydeus fighting, marries his daughters Argia and Deipyle to them in response to a prophecy, and promises to restore them to their homelands. He gathers and leads the Seven Champions against Thebes, is stationed at the Homoloidian Gate, and wins at Nemea. Sole survivor of the Argives, he is saved by Arion, flees to Athens, and seeks burial for the Argive dead.

Thebes is a city and the place where Cadmus founded a settlement when a guiding cow collapsed, after killing the dragon at the spring of Ares and sowing its teeth. Named after Thebe, it contains the dragon’s teeth and later endures the Teumessian vixen, for which the Thebans expose a citizen’s son each month. Amphitryon, Alcmena, and Licymnius go there, and Amphitryon is purified there. Thebes owes Erginus tribute until Hercules defeats Erginus and the Minyans, then makes the Minyans pay double tribute to Thebes. Dionysus comes there and drives its women to Bacchic frenzy on Cithaeron. Its rule passes through Polydorus, Lycus, Zethus and Amphion, Laius, Creon, Oedipus, Eteocles, and Creon again. The Sphinx afflicts it until Oedipus solves her riddle. After Polynices is banished, Argives attack its seven gates; the Thebans defend it, but Eteocles and Polynices die. Finally, after attacks by Athenians and the Epigoni and the flight of its inhabitants, Argives enter, take booty, and destroy its walls.
Son of Astacus, Melanippus wounds Tydeus in the belly, then Amphiaraus cuts off his head and gives it to Tydeus.

Alcmaeon, son of Eriphyle, leads the Epigoni against Thebes after Apollo predicts victory and kills Laodamas. Obeying Apollo, he kills Eriphyle and is pursued by her Fury. Purified by Phegeus and Achelous, he marries Arsinoe, later Callirrhoe, colonizes Acarnania, and is killed by the sons of Phegeus.

Telephus, son of Auge and Hercules, is exposed as a babe on Mount Parthenius, suckled by a doe, and raised by the herdsmen of Corythus. On reaching maturity he seeks his parents at Delphi. After receiving the god’s information, he travels to Mysia, becomes Teuthras’s adopted son, succeeds him on his death, and rules Mysia.
Nephele, mother of Phrixus and Helle, receives a golden-fleeced ram from Hermes, rescues her children from the altar, and sends them through the sky on it.

Phrixus, son of Athamas and Nephele and brother of Helle, is brought to an altar for sacrifice to Zeus. Nephele rescues him; he crosses land and sea by a golden-fleeced ram to the Colchians, marries Chalciope, has four sons, sacrifices the ram to Zeus, and gives its fleece to Aeetes.
Helle, daughter of Athamas and Nephele, is carried by a golden-fleeced ram over the sea, slips off, drowns, and dies.

Ino, daughter of Cadmus and Harmonia, becomes Athamas’s second wife and mother of Learchus and Melicertes. She plots to have Phrixus sacrificed by parching wheat and bribing Delphi’s messengers. Later she plunges into the sea with her dead child and is known as Leucothoe.
Given by Nephele to Phrixus and Helle, it carries them through the sky; Phrixus sacrifices it to Zeus, and its golden fleece goes to Aeetes.
is_named_after Helle [because she was drowned there] The sea where Helle drowns is thereafter called the Hellespont after her.

The Colchians are people sent by Aeetes to find the Argo and Medea under threat of Medea’s punishment. They disperse in search: some settle in Corcyra, near the Ceraunian mountains, or on the Apsyrtides Islands; others reach the Phaeacians, demand Medea, then settle there.

Aeetes is king of the Colchians and ruler of Colchis, child of Sun by Perseis, sibling of Circe and Pasiphae, and father of Medea and Chalciope. He receives Phrixus, gives Chalciope to him, and receives and safeguards the Golden Fleece, nailing it to an oak in a grove of Ares. When Jason seeks the fleece, Aeetes sets tasks involving brazen-footed bulls and dragon’s teeth, then refuses the fleece and seeks to destroy the Argo and its crew. He pursues Medea and Jason, falls behind while recovering and burying Apsyrtus’ limbs, and sends searchers after them. Perses deposes him, but Medea kills Perses and restores his kingdom.
Pasiphae, daughter of Perseis and the Sun and wife of Minos, is made to desire a bull, uses a wooden cow with Daedalus’s help, and gives birth to the Minotaur.

Minos, son of Europa by Zeus, is a prince and later king of Crete. After Poseidon sends a bull in response to his prayer, he sacrifices another instead. He marries Pasiphae, fathers children, gives Procris a magical dog, makes laws, confines the Minotaur, and recovers Glaucus after his restoration.
Argus was the son of Niobe and Zeus. After receiving the kingdom, he named the Peloponnese Argos after himself, married Evadne, and fathered Ecbasus, Peirantes, Epidaurus, and Criassus.

is_ruled_by Creon [kingdom] Jason and Medea settle in Corinth and live happily there for ten years. Their relationship ends when Jason marries Glauce, and Corinth becomes the scene of Medea’s revenge against Glauce, Creon, Mermerus, and Pheres.
Glaucus, son of Minos by Pasiphae, dies after falling into a jar of honey while chasing a mouse, then Polyidus restores him with an herb brought by a serpent.

Bellerophon, son of Glaucus, seeks purification after accidentally killing a relative, rejects Stheneboea, survives Iobates’s tasks by killing Chimera and Lycians, then marries Philonoe and inherits Iobates’s kingdom.

A fire-breathing monster with lion forepart, goat middle head, and dragon tail, begotten by Typhon on Echidna and bred by Amisodares; it devastated country and cattle until Bellerophon, riding Pegasus, shot it down from height.
Cephalus, son of Deioneus from Thoricus in Attica, joins Amphitryon with Laelaps, receives Tafian booty, and settles in a city founded under his name.

Perseus, a hero and Danae’s son, was cast into the sea with her, rescued and raised by Dictys, then sent by Polydectes for the Gorgon’s head. Guided by Hermes and Athena and equipped with sickle, shield, wallet, cap, and sandals, he beheaded Medusa. In Ethiopia he killed a sea monster, rescued Andromeda, and fathered her children. Using the head, he turned Phineus’s conspirators and Polydectes’s friends to stone, installed Dictys as king, and gave it to Athena. After accidentally killing Acrisius, he exchanged Argos for Tiryns with Megapenthes, ruled there, and fortified Midea and Mycenae.
Polydectes, king of Seriphus and Dictys’s brother, loves Danae and contrives to send the grown Perseus after the Gorgon’s head.
Dictys, brother of Polydectes, takes a chest reaching Seriphus and raises Perseus from it.
Seriphus was the place where the chest came ashore. Polydectes ruled there, and Dictys raised Perseus there.

Tyro, daughter of Salmoneus and Alcidice, is raised by Cretheus, loves Enipeus, and bears Pelias and Neleus after Poseidon approaches as Enipeus. She exposes them; grown, they recognize her and kill Sidero for ill-treating her.

Pelias, Tyro’s twin son and Neleus’s brother, was exposed as an infant, marked on the face by a mare, and raised by horse-keepers. After recognizing Tyro, he and Neleus killed their stepmother Sidero. He lived in Thessaly, became king of Iolcus after Cretheus, and was father of Acastus, Alcestis, and other daughters; accounts name Anaxibia or Phylomache as his wife. He offered Alcestis to whoever could yoke a lion and boar, a condition Admetus met. Warned against the one-sandaled man, he recognized Jason and ordered him to seek the Golden Fleece from Colchis. He later despaired of the Argonauts and sought Aeson’s death. Accounts differ: he died from bull’s blood during sacrifice, or Medea deceived his daughters into killing him; Acastus buried him and expelled Jason and Medea.

Neleus, Tyro’s son and Pelias’s twin, was exposed, rescued, and raised by horse-keepers. After helping kill Sidero, he quarreled with Pelias and was banished, then lived in Messene, founded and ruled Pylus, married Chloris, fathered children, and was killed by Hercules at Pylus.
is_a city [taken by Hercules] Pylus was founded by Neleus in Messene. Heracles later ravaged Pylus, killing Neleus’s sons except Nestor.

Amphion, son of Antiope and Zeus, is exposed with Zethus but raised by a neatherd. Given a lyre by Hermes, he practises minstrelsy and helps fortify Thebes as stones follow his music. After recognizing Antiope, he and Zethus kill Lycus; he later succeeds to Thebes, marries Niobe, dies, and Laius takes the kingdom.
Nestor, son of Neleus, alone survives Heracles’s attack on Pylus after being raised among the Gerenians; he marries Anaxibia and fathers Pisidice, Antilochus, and other children.
Bias, son of Amythaon and brother of Melampus, sought Pero; after Melampus obtained Phylacus’s kine, Bias married Pero and became father of Talaus.

Alcestis, daughter of Pelias and wife of Admetus, is defined by voluntarily dying in Admetus’s place when his parents would not. Admetus obtained her after yoking a lion and boar to a car. After her death, she is restored, either by Persephone or by Hercules after fighting Hades.

Melampus is an excellent soothsayer and seer, son of Amythaon and Idmene, who gains understanding of birds and divination through Apollo, birds, and snakes that purge his ears. Imprisoned after stealing Phylacus’s kine, he learns from a vulture how Iphiclus may have children and secures the kine for Bias’s marriage to Pero. He devises cures with drugs and purifications, heals Proetus’s daughters and the mad women of Argos, gains part of the sovereignty, and settles there with Bias.
Eteocles resorted to divination to learn how the Thebans might overcome the Argives. Tiresias, who was a seer, is then described in connection with prophetic knowledge.

are_guarded_by guard dog [in Phylace] The kine of Phylacus were guarded by a dog that no person or beast could approach. Melampus stole them for Bias, was detected and imprisoned for a year, and then drove the kine to Pylus so that Bias could receive Pero.
Aristomachus, son of Cleodaeus, leads a later return attempt after earlier failures, then is defeated and killed by the Peloponnesians.

Eriphyle’s agreed decisions settle disputes between Amphiaraus and Adrastus. Bribed with Polynices’ necklace, she persuades Amphiaraus to march; later, after receiving a robe from Thersander, she persuades her sons to join the expedition. Alcmaeon learns she was bribed and, following Apollo’s instruction, kills her, alone or with Amphilochus.
The Epigoni, sons of Argive dead, marched against Thebes ten years later to avenge their fathers, choosing Alcmaeon as leader.

is_ruled_by Lycurgus [when the champions arrive] Nemea is ruled by Lycurgus. The champions come there seeking water, and events there include the death and burial of Opheltes and the establishment of the Nemean Games.
Opheltes, infant son of Eurydice and Lycurgus nursed by Hypsipyle, is killed by a serpent after she leaves him; champions bury and rename him Archemorus.
is_a name of Opheltes [given after his death] Archemorus is the name given to Opheltes after his death. Amphiaraus says that the child's death is a sign foretelling the future.

Medea is a witch and sorceress, daughter of Aeetes and Idyia and younger sister of Apsyrtus. Loving Jason, she helps him yoke bulls and take the fleece by drugging its dragon, then flees with him and Apsyrtus, whom she kills and dismembers. She aids Jason’s revenge on Pelias, but after Jason divorces her in Corinth, she kills Glauce, Creon, Mermerus, and Pheres and escapes to Athens. There she marries Aegeus and bears Medus, plots against Theseus, and is expelled with Medus. Returning unknown to Colchis, she kills Perses and restores Aeetes’ kingdom.

Colchis is a realm of Aeetes, containing the Phasis River and a grove of Ares where the Golden Fleece hangs from an oak, guarded by a sleepless dragon. The Argonauts arrive; Jason asks Aeetes for and is sent to obtain the fleece. Later Medea comes there unknown after leaving Athens.

The Golden Fleece is a fleece in Colchis, hung on an oak in a grove of Ares and guarded by a sleepless dragon. Pelias orders Jason to bring it back. Jason seeks it, while Aeetes sets tasks involving brazen-footed bulls and dragon’s teeth and later refuses it. Medea leads Jason to the fleece, helps overcome the dragon, and escapes with it to the Argo. Jason returns to Iolcus and gives it to Pelias.

The Argonauts are Greek nobles and heroes assembled for Jason’s expedition to the Golden Fleece, serving as the crew of the Argo, with Hercules among them. They sail from Greece, stop at Lemnos, mistakenly fight the Doliones, and leave Hercules and Polyphemus in Mysia. After aiding Phineus and passing the Clashing Rocks, they reach Colchis and support Jason’s tasks. Following the fleece’s taking, they flee with Medea and Apsyrtus, are purified by Circe, survive further dangers, and reach Iolcus after four months.

Argo is a ship of fifty oars, built and named by Argus, son of Phrixus, and fitted by Athena with speaking timber from Dodona’s oak in its prow. It carries Jason and the Argonauts toward Colchis, leaves while Hercules and Polyphemus search for Hylas, reaches Salmydessus, and passes the Clashing Rocks after its prow releases a dove and its fittings are cut. It then bears Jason, Medea, Apsyrtus, and the Argonauts fleeing Colchis, speaks near the Apsyrtides, is guided by Thetis and the Nereids, and is dedicated by Jason to Poseidon at the Isthmus.
Aleus was a son of Aphidas. By Neaera, he had a daughter, Auge, and two sons, Cepheus and Lycurgus.
Erginus marches against Thebes after Hercules mutilates his heralds. Hercules kills Erginus, defeats the Minyans, and reverses the tribute imposed on Thebes.

Augeas is king of Elis, with many cattle herds. He agrees to give Hercules a tenth of them if Hercules cleans the dung in one day, doubting he can do it. Afterward, he denies the promise, expels Hercules and Phyleus, appoints generals against Hercules, and is killed when Hercules captures Elis; Phyleus receives the kingdom.

Polyphemus, son of Elatus, hears Hylas cry out in Mysia and searches with Hercules after mistaking the danger for robbers. Left behind when the Argo departs, he founds Cius in Mysia and reigns there as king.
Elatus, a centaur son of Arcas and Leaneira, held power over his land share, married Laodice, and fathered Stymphalus and Pereus.

Hypsipyle, Thoas’s daughter, ruled Lemnos after its men were gone, saving her father while others killed fathers and husbands. She slept with Jason and bore Euneus and Nebrophonus. Later, as a purchased bondwoman in Lycurgus’s house, she led champions to water, leaving infant Opheltes, who was killed by a serpent.

The Lemnian women, cursed with a noisome smell after dishonoring Aphrodite, kill their fathers and husbands after the men sleep with Thracian captives; Hypsipyle saves her father, and they later receive and sleep with the Argonauts.

Mysia is a land visited by the Argonauts after Lemnos and before the Bebrycian land. After Cyzicus was buried, they stopped there; Hercules and Polyphemus remained searching for Hylas, and Polyphemus founded and ruled Cius. Teuthras ruled Mysia before Telephus succeeded him.
Hylas, son of Thiodamas and beloved by Hercules, is sent to draw water in Mysia, abducted by nymphs for his beauty, and sought by Hercules and Polyphemus.
Omphale, daughter of Iardanes and queen of Lydia, buys Hercules from Hermes after an oracle orders his sale; he serves her as a slave for three years, performing deeds.

l: marriage of Admetus and Alcestis, The Library
s: includes sacrifice [at which Artemis was omitted] At the marriage of Admetus and Alcestis, Admetus forgot to sacrifice to Artemis. When he opened the marriage chamber, he found it filled with coils of snakes, and Apollo told him to appease the goddess.

l: oracle of the one-sandaled man, The Library
s: warns Pelias [to beware of the man with a single sandal] The oracle warned Pelias to beware of the man with a single sandal. Pelias initially failed to understand it but later recognized its meaning when Jason arrived wearing only one sandal.

identifies Jason [as the man of Pelias’s oracle] Jason lost one sandal while crossing the Anaurus and emerged from the river wearing only one. This fulfilled the sign in the oracle that Pelias should beware of the one-sandaled man.

allows Alcestis [to die voluntarily in Admetus’s stead] Apollo obtained from the Fates the condition that Admetus could escape death if someone voluntarily died for him. When the appointed day came, neither Admetus's father nor his mother agreed to die, but Alcestis did so.

The voyage of the Argo, led by Jason, begins when he gathers the Argonauts to seek the Golden Fleece in Colchis. It visits Lemnos, where Jason sleeps with Hypsipyle, then the Doliones and Mysia, leaving Hercules and Polyphemus behind searching for Hylas.

l: massacre of the Lemnian men, The Library
s: causes Lemnos [to be bereft of men] The Lemnian women killed their fathers and husbands after being dishonored by their husbands' intercourse with captive women from Thrace. Hypsipyle alone saved her own father, Thoas, by hiding him.
Phineus, a blind seer living at Salmydessus and said by one tradition to be Poseidon’s child, suffers Harpies sent by gods; freed by Argonauts, he guides their voyage past the Clashing Rocks.

The Harpies are winged female creatures sent by the gods to Phineus. They repeatedly steal most food from his table and leave a stench-filled remainder. Zetes and Calais pursue them through the air; one falls into the river Tigres, while the other reaches the Echinadian Islands. They include several differently named Harpies.

The Wandering Rocks, also called Planctae and Cyaneae, are huge sea cliffs that clash in winds and block passage. Following Phineus’s advice, the Argonauts send a dove, then row through with Hera’s help; after their ship passes, the rocks stand still.
Lycus, king of the Mariandynians and Nycteus’s brother, flees after killing Phlegyas, rules Thebes for twenty years, captures Antiope, and is killed by Zethus and Amphion.
Two enormous wild bulls, gifted by Hephaestus, have bronze feet and breathe fire; Jason, protected by Medea’s drug, yokes them.
Dragon’s teeth, sown by Cadmus on Athena’s advice after he killed the dragon, produced armed men called the Sparti, who fought one another.

Cadmus, son of Agenor and Telephassa, though alternatively of Phoenix, is sent to seek Europa. Guided by a cow, he founds Thebes, kills Ares’s dragon, sows its teeth, and serves Ares for an eternal year in atonement. He receives the kingdom and marries Harmonia, possessing her necklace and robe. Leaving Thebes with her, he aids the Encheleans, defeats the Illyrians, and reigns over them. After Illyrius is born, Zeus transforms Cadmus and Harmonia into serpents and sends him to the Elysian Fields.
A magical substance Medea gives Jason; he anoints his shield, spear, and body with it, gaining one day’s protection from fire and iron.

l: Jason and Medea’s marriage pact, The Library
s: Jason and Medea make a conditional marriage agreement: Medea will help him and give him the Golden Fleece, while Jason swears to marry her and take her to Greece.

l: yoking the bulls and sowing the dragon’s teeth, The Library
s: is_a task assigned to Jason [required by Aeetes] Aeetes requires Jason to yoke the brazen-footed bulls and sow the dragon’s teeth. After Jason sows the teeth, armed men rise from the ground; he throws stones among them so that they fight one another, then approaches and kills them.

is_sibling_of Medea [brother] Apsyrtus accompanies Medea and Jason aboard the Argo when they flee by night. Medea kills him, cuts him into pieces, and throws them into the sea. His murder causes Zeus to send a storm and requires the Argonauts to be purified by Circe.

l: the murder of Apsyrtus, The Library
s: causes the purification for Apsyrtus’s murder [required by Zeus’s wrath] The murder of Apsyrtus is committed by Medea while Aeetes pursues the fleeing Argo. Zeus responds with anger and a storm, and the Argonauts must travel to Ausonia to be purified by Circe for the deed.

Talos is a bronze man, though some call him a bull, who guards Crete by circling it three times daily. With a single vein sealed by a bronze nail, he prevents the Argonauts from landing and pelts the Argo with stones. Medea causes his death through drugs, removal of the nail, or an ankle shot.
Iolcus, ruled by Pelias, receives the Argonauts and fleece; after Pelias dies, Acastus expels Jason and Medea.

Creon is a ruler and father: son of Menoeceus, father of Glauce, king of Corinth, and successor to Laius in Thebes. After Laius’s burial, he ruled Thebes, offered its kingdom and Laius’s wife Jocasta to whoever solved the Sphinx’s riddle, and lost Haemon to the Sphinx. He purified and aided Amphitryon after the Cadmea was freed of the vixen, joining the attack on the Tafian islands. Later he forbade burial of Argive dead, set watchmen, and had Antigone interred alive for burying Polynices. In Corinth he betrothed Glauce to Jason and died rescuing her from her poisoned robe’s fire.
Glauce, Creon’s daughter, becomes Jason’s wife after his divorce from Medea, then dies when Medea’s poisoned robe burns her in fierce fire.
Mermerus is one of the children Medea has with Jason. Medea kills him before fleeing Corinth.

Athens, led by Theseus, receives suppliants: Medea, the sons of Hercules, and Adrastus. It protects the sons of Hercules against Eurystheus, then marches with Theseus against Thebes, captures it, and delivers the Argive dead to their kinsfolk for burial. Medea is later driven away with Medus.
Medus, son of Medea and Aegeus, was expelled from Athens with Medea, conquered barbarians, named Media, and died campaigning against Indians.
Media was the name Medus gave to the whole country under his control after he conquered many barbarians.
Inachus, son of Ocean and Tethys, fathers Phoroneus and Aegialeus with Melia; a river in Argos is named after him.

Niobe is described as a daughter of Tantalus, and elsewhere of Phoroneus and Teledice; she bears Argus, and according to Acusilaus Pelasgus, by Zeus, and marries Amphion. With seven sons and seven daughters in one account, she claims superiority over Latona, provoking Artemis and Apollo, prays to Zeus, and becomes a weeping stone at Sipylus.
Pelasgus, father of Lycaon, is said by Acusilaus to be son of Zeus and Niobe, and by Hesiod to have been born from the soil.

Argus the All-seeing, descended from Ecbasus through Agenor and also described as Arestor’s son or earthborn, had eyes throughout his body. He killed threats including a bull ravaging Arcadia, a satyr, Tartarus, Echidna, and Apis’s killers, wearing the bull’s hide. Hera made him guardian of Io, a white cow; after tethering her near Mycenae, he was killed by Hermes.
Iasus, spouse of Clymene, is presented as Atalanta’s father, though other accounts name Schoeneus; one tradition also makes him Io’s father.

Io, a priestess of Hera, was seduced by Zeus and changed into a white cow. Guarded by Argus and tormented by Hera’s gadfly, she wandered through Europe and Asia. In Egypt she regained human form, bore Epaphus, married Telegonus after finding him in Syria, and was identified with Isis.

Epaphus, son of Io, was born beside the Nile after Io regained her form, disappeared at Hera’s request and was found by Io; he reigned over the Egyptians, married Memphis, founded Memphis, and fathered Libya.
Libya, daughter of Epaphus, bears Poseidon's twin sons Belus and Agenor.
